<reason>CON won by repeatedly narrowing the clash and turning PRO's own materials against it. CON flipped the calculator analogy (permission arrived after the skill was internalized), showed that PRO's real safeguard was oral defense rather than disclosure and that oral defense works under either default while being unscalable at thirty students per section, and then used its pressure question to force PRO into saying the honestly-disclosing heavy user fails—which CON immediately converted into a self-incrimination problem that collapses PRO's honesty dividend. CON's closing isolated the decisive "middle zone" student who outsources the thinking but keeps the typing and is compliant only under PRO's default; PRO never squarely answered that framing, the overhead point, or the norm-shaping argument about the marginal student. PRO kept a genuine live route—the ban cannot see anything, and a log at least gives the honest process-user a reason to come forward—and its "banned empty room is an A with no receipt" line was its strongest moment, but it defended rather than advanced, and its exception ("when unaided sentences are the object") conceded the core skill for most pre-college essays. CON's clipped final rebuttal was a minor execution cost that did not change the outcome.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5–B4.7: after PRO answered Q1 by saying the honestly-disclosed heavy user receives incomplete credit, CON showed that this makes heavy disclosure a grade-costing confession, so rational heavy users lie in the log exactly as they would under a ban—"the secrecy PRO promised to end returns, now with a form to falsify"—reducing PRO's policy to restriction of the core skill plus paperwork. PRO's closing reply (light process-users still disclose because it earns credit) was reasonable but left the middle-zone problem unanswered.</best_rebuttal>
